notes: \cpara{An epigraph with a joke: in the original the credit to Dante is struck through (shown here between tildes), and Kennedy is labeled a ``misquoter.'' The joke is accurate. Wikiquote traces the line to Henry Powell Spring (1944), popularized by Kennedy as Dante's; Dante put those who were neither for nor against God near the mouth of Hell, not in its hottest place.}

\cpara{Names the target: neutrality or suspended judgment displayed ``in order to signal maturity, impartiality, or a superior vantage point.'' ``Attire'' and ``profess'' refer back to ``Belief as Attire'' and ``Professing and Cheering,'' from August 2007.}

\cpara{The first example, told at more length in ``Against Maturity,'' posted the day before. There the parents' reply is given as ``Only children ask questions like that; when you're adult, you know that it's pointless to argue about it.'' And there the author's explanation, offered as ``what I think my parents were thinking,'' is a story the parents told themselves: having given up on such questions, they ``labeled `mature' the place and act of giving up, by way of consolation.'' Here the reply appears as a display aimed at others.}

\cpara{The principal's sentence has a second half that the paragraph does not discuss: ``it only matters who ends it.'' Read as addressed to the children, it tells each of them that stopping, not hitting back, is what will count. That is a reason about the children's conduct, not the adults' convenience. The paragraph explains the sentence by the adults' convenience and gives no evidence that this is why principals say it.}

\cpara{Extends the principal's case to Great Powers, with ``I believe'' and no case named except a sarcastic one-liner. ``Oh, can't Israel and Hamas just get along?'' was posted a month after the Gaza War, which ran from 27 December 2008 to 18 January 2009 (Wikipedia). The post does not say which demands for a truce it has in mind, or who made them.}

\cpara{Names the pattern, and defines it by motive: ``trying to signal wisdom by refusing to make guesses.'' The refusal can be seen; the wish to signal wisdom cannot, and the post gives no way to tell pretended neutrality from sincere neutrality. (``Professing and Cheering'' and ``Belief as Attire'' have the same gap; see the notes there.)}

\cpara{Quotes Paulo Freire, then applies his line to playgrounds and to international politics: when those in charge do not care who started a fight, aggressors gain. I could not check the quotation against the book.}
\clogic{That a policy suits the people who follow it does not show that they follow it because it suits them. The post gives no case in which that is shown.}

\cpara{Adds a second motive, status: a principal who took sides would sink to ``a mere participant in the fray.'' Like the first motive, it is supported only by imagining what ``other adults'' would think.}

\cpara{Extends the pattern to the ``revered elder'' whose reputation for fairness depends on refusing to pass judgment. ``Almost always in vain'' is a general claim with no example. The footnote adds the obvious counterexample, judges.}
\cpara{Grants that suspending judgment is sometimes rational, and introduces a comment by Michael Rooney on ``Knowing About Biases Can Hurt People'' (April 2007).}
\cpara{Rooney's point: students given reasons to suspend judgment conclude instead that every judgment is as plausible as any other.}
\cpara{Names the related fault, claiming that the evidence is balanced when it is not, with a sample remark about natural selection and intelligent design.}
\cpara{The post's strongest point, and a correct one: to say that the evidence is balanced is to make a claim about the evidence, which can be checked and can be wrong like any other claim.}
\cpara{Applies the point to policy: a call for compromise on abortion is a position, ``every bit as particular'' as either side's.}

\cpara{Advises practicing on less charged topics than abortion or the Israeli--Palestinian conflict. The author's ``Politics is the Mind-Killer'' (February 2007) went further: to make a point about rationality, avoid contemporary politics ``if you can possibly avoid it,'' and if the point ``is inherently about politics, then talk about Louis XVI during the French Revolution.'' This post uses abortion and the Gaza fighting of the previous weeks, although its playground example makes the point without politics.}

\cpara{Allows a second, legitimate reason to stay out of a dispute, from Robin Hanson: divisive conversations are costly, so one may spend effort on neglected questions instead (``pull the rope sideways''). Hanson's two posts in the footnote support the paraphrase.}
\cpara{Concludes that setting an issue aside is a matter of limited resources, not of a higher vantage point.}
\cpara{Sums up with three items. The third, pretending that neutrality or abstention shows superior wisdom, is the post's target.}
\cpara{The source of the Freire quotation. I could not reach the book.}
\cpara{Notes that judges give verdicts without losing their reputation for impartiality, and offers two guesses why, each introduced with ``Maybe.''}
